title: Namdev

segments.voice: Yesterday, the boy Namdev set a bowl of milk before Vitthal and waited until, the story says, the god drank it. What did you give and stay to see received? Day nine hundred seventeen.

A potter walks slowly down a row of seated saints, holding the flat wooden paddle he uses on pots. He taps a pot, he listens: is it fired all the way through, or still soft inside? The story says Jnaneshwar asked him, Gora the potter, to test the devotees gathered there. So Gora taps each head in turn. Each saint sits quietly and takes it. Then he reaches Namdev, and Namdev bristles. He's offended, and he says so. Gora listens to the sound, and gives his verdict to the whole room. This pot is still half-baked.
screen: `GORA THE POTTER.` → `HE TAPS EACH HEAD.` → `THIS POT IS HALF-BAKED.`

segments.voice: That verdict stung, because Namdev's love for Vitthal was real. This is the boy whose milk, the story says, Vitthal drank, and who grew up talking to him like a friend. So Namdev runs to Vitthal to complain. And Vitthal, in the story, takes the potter's side. You have love, he says. What you don't have yet is a teacher. Go and find Visoba Khechar. Namdev finds the old man in a Shiva temple, lying down, apparently asleep, with his feet resting on the linga, the stone that stands for Shiva. Namdev is shocked and wakes him. Visoba answers mildly. I'm old and tired. Lift my feet, please, and set them down somewhere God is not. So Namdev lifts the feet and moves them. A linga rises up under them. He moves them again. Another. Wherever the feet come down, Shiva is already there. At last Namdev sets them down in his own lap, and he understands. There is nowhere to put the feet, because there is nowhere without God. Look at what was wrong with the pot. Not too little devotion. Devotion with walls around it, so fond of God in one image, in one town, that it couldn't hear him anywhere else. The potter heard the hollow place. The teacher didn't argue about it. He handed Namdev a puzzle he could only solve with his hands. Look back at this week. Sambandar pointed at the sky. Jnaneshwar touched a buffalo's head and asked a wall to move. And Namdev, humbled by a potter, learned from a man who seemed to be breaking every rule that the holy was already under his hands.
screen: `A POTTER CALLS HIM HALF-BAKED.` · `VITTHAL SAYS: FIND A TEACHER.` · `FEET ON THE LINGA.` · then, large: `NOWHERE TO PUT THE FEET.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your breath settle into its own pace. Choose one place you'll be later today that feels ordinary, even dull: a bus seat, a sink full of dishes, a desk, a waiting room. Bring it clearly to mind, the light, the sounds, the smell of it. Now, the way Namdev set down those tired feet, set your attention down there, gently, and ask: what if this place is not empty of what I call holy? You don't need an answer. Just let the ordinary place stay in mind a little longer than usual. If you pray, you can hold that place before God. The bell holds the time.
Namdev. The poet-saint of Pandharpur, called half-baked by a potter, who learned from Visoba Khechar that there's nowhere to put the feet where God is not.
Your line: Namdev. Today, when you land somewhere you'd call nowhere special, tap it like Gora's pot and listen for a moment. Day nine hundred seventeen.

howItsDone: The stories of Gora the potter and Visoba Khechar belong to the Varkari tradition of Maharashtra, whose members sing the songs of Namdev and the other saints of Pandharpur in praise of Vitthal.

fork.setup: you're Namdev. an old man lies with his feet on the Shiva linga, and asks you to set them down somewhere God is not. what do you do?
options: refuse and walk out of the temple.
lift his feet and set them down somewhere else.
go and fetch the temple priest.
fork.reveal: he moves them again and again, and a linga rises under them each time, until he understands there's nowhere without God.

trapdoor: what you thought: a potter insults a saint.
what it means: Namdev's love was real but walled in, and Visoba's feet showed him there's nowhere without God.
what a scholar hears: Varkari memory names Visoba Khechar as Namdev's guru, so the boy who talked with Vitthal still needed a human teacher.
